title: Harmlessness
hookLine: the intention not to harm, even in thought

cards: Credit for an idea gets taken in a meeting, and on the drive home a little film starts to play. In it, the person who took it trips on the stairs. Their coffee spills down their shirt.
Their car gets a flat in the rain. Nobody is badly hurt, of course. Just enough.
Nobody acts on it. A film like that can run for a long time before anyone notices it's running. The Buddha noticed.

Before his awakening, he says, he caught thoughts of harming in his own mind and put them in the bad pile, right beside ill will. Today, the last of the three right intentions: harmlessness, all the way down into thought.

teach.h: AVIHIṂSĀ: THE INTENTION NOT TO HARM.
teach.b: The word on our list is ahimsa, a word Pali and Sanskrit share: the not-harming that Jains and Hindus hold dear as well. In the Pali list of right intentions, the word is avihiṃsā, non-cruelty: the intention not to harm.
Goodwill was about not wishing ill. This one leans closer to action: not wanting anyone to suffer, and not wanting to be the cause.

In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, when a thought of harming arose in him, the Buddha saw that it led to his own affliction, to others', or to both, and away from wisdom. As he considered that, it subsided.
So harm starts upstream, in the film, long before a hand moves.

The Dhammapada gives the reason in one line, in Max Müller's words: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." You are like them.
That's the whole argument. A later verse says a person isn't called noble for injuring living creatures, but for having pity on all of them.
Later teachers pair harmlessness with compassion, karuṇā: it's the soil compassion grows in. Look back at the week. The blind men, each holding a part.
Intend it. Two piles. Guard, then rest.
The relief of less. Steer by goodwill.
And today, no harm meant. Three right intentions, one direction.

how: Lay Buddhists take the first precept, not to kill, as the outward form of harmlessness; some also reflect on verses like Dhammapada 129 or practice compassion meditation toward beings who suffer.

o: not harming: the intention to cause no pain
a strict diet that avoids all meat
refusing to fight back in any situation

games.q: what's inside harmlessness: tap the pairs.
p: remember that you are like unto them

s: in this teaching, harmlessness begins only with what you do
MN 19 traces harm back to thoughts, which afflict oneself, others, or both.
the word ahimsa is honored by Jains and Hindus too
not harming is a shared ideal among India's traditions.
the Dhammapada calls a person noble for having pity on all living creatures
verse 270: not for injuring living creatures, but for pity toward all of them.

games.q: someone has wronged you, and the little film is running. what reason does Dhammapada 129 give for not harming them?
o: they tremble at punishment and fear death, just as you do.
games.why: the verse rests on likeness, not on fear or rules: all fear death, so remember that you are like unto them.

practice: Gently look for the film: is there anyone you've been quietly wishing a small misfortune on, a coworker, a neighbor, someone on the news?

Don't scold yourself for finding it; just catch it, the way you'd catch a glass before it hits the floor. Then do what the Dhammapada suggests, remember they're like you, they flinch at pain too, and let the film stop there.

wordCard.voice: Ahimsa. Not harming. In the Buddha's list it's avihiṃsā, the intention not to harm, the third right intention.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali ahiṃsā: not harming; the Pali right-intention list uses its close cousin avihiṃsā, non-cruelty.

carryVoice: Your line: no harm meant. A film can end unfinished. One more week on the path, complete.
